text:
The flat had two bedrooms, though Daniel never entered the second. The first contained a mattress standing on its side. In the kitchen, a refrigerator hummed as though nobody had told it the household was over.

Rachel usually met him at the door.

“We ought to do something about this place,” she would say.

Sometimes she was thirty-two, the age at which they had married. Sometimes she had the practical haircut acquired during their separation. She was never angry. This was one of the dream’s more disturbing features.

They still had the flat. They were still paying for it. Neither of them lived there.

On waking, Daniel experienced several seconds of a property owner’s alarm. Then the room resolved itself: the leaning wardrobe, the streetlamp through the curtains, Isabel asleep beside him. He owned no secret flat. In London, this should have been a disappointment. Instead, it was a relief.

The dream had been recurring for nearly a year.

He had initially assigned it to the same department as missed trains and examinations for which he had neglected to prepare. But the flat acquired details: a stain above the cooker, a window painted shut. Once a letter arrived addressed to both of them, and he spent the dream wondering whether opening it would make them responsible for something.

He did not tell Isabel.

They had been together six years, long enough for secrecy to become distinguishable from privacy. Daniel believed in privacy, particularly when it saved him from explaining something that became less intelligible in the explaining.

One Saturday, over breakfast, Isabel said, “You were apologizing in your sleep.”

“Was I?”

“Quite formally. I wondered whether I should accept.”

He put down his toast.

This was how he finally told her: between the marmalade and a discussion about the boiler.

“And Rachel’s always there?” she asked.

“Almost.”

“What happens?”

“We discuss what to do with the flat.”

“What do you do?”

“Nothing.”

Isabel turned her mug by its handle.

“Is it nice?”

“Potentially.”

“Of course. The most expensive kind.”

He smiled, but her expression had not committed itself to amusement.

“I don’t think it’s about wanting her back.”

“I didn’t say it was.”

“No.”

“Would you know?”

He considered this.

“I think so.”

She took his plate when she took her own, though he had not finished eating.

Daniel and Rachel had divorced eleven years earlier. They had no children or continuing financial arrangements. She lived in Bristol with a man who designed hospital equipment. He knew this from an email sent when his mother died: kind, specific, and without invitations to continue the correspondence.

Their marriage had ended without a discovery. They had simply become proficient at disappointing one another.

Rachel wanted decisions made. Daniel wanted them to emerge from sufficient consideration, preferably so gradually that nobody could identify the person responsible. When they looked at houses, he found defects. When they discussed holidays, he suggested October. By October, it was too late.

With Isabel he had tried to be different. He booked restaurants. He agreed to the sofa. He had learned that enthusiasm could precede certainty.

Still, on Sunday, when she asked whether he wanted to see a film, he said, “Let me see how I get on.”

“With what?”

He looked at the newspaper around him.

“A few things.”

“Right.”

After she left, he read the same paragraph three times.

That evening, washing dishes, Isabel told him she sometimes dreamed about her former husband.

“We’re usually driving somewhere. He won’t ask directions.”

“Did he ever?”

“He was excellent at asking directions. That’s what’s annoying.”

She dried a glass.

“After we separated, I used to dream we’d had a child.”

Daniel turned off the tap.

“You never told me.”

“No.”

“What was it like?”

“The child? I never saw it. I was always trying to get back to wherever we’d left it.”

“Peter didn’t want children.”

“By the end, neither did I. That doesn’t mean I didn’t want the life in which we wanted them.”

He watched her fold the tea towel. He knew the account of her marriage as one knows a journey somebody else has taken: the principal stops, where the trouble began. It had not occurred to him that she still visited it.

“Do you mind about Rachel?”

“A little.”

“I’m sorry.”

“I don’t need you to be sorry for being asleep.”

He waited.

“What I mind is that you’ve been worrying for a year, and I’ve been here.”

The following Saturday they cleaned the hall cupboard. Isabel denied any symbolic intention.

Behind four umbrellas and a tennis racket belonging to neither of them was a cardboard box marked SORT in Daniel’s handwriting.

It contained appliance manuals, foreign coins, a photograph of Rachel’s father holding a fish, and an envelope of keys.

One brass key was attached to a cork float with a faded red stripe.

“Oh,” Isabel said. “Wales.”

Then he remembered: a gravel drive, rain stippling a lake, Isabel in a borrowed yellow waterproof.

Their first holiday.

The cottage smelled of ashes. On the second morning, the owner offered them a canoe.

“There’s no point waiting for it to stop.”

The key opened the boathouse.

Daniel remembered objecting that the sky looked bad. Isabel had surveyed the uniform grey.

“In what direction?”

They carried the canoe down a slippery slope. Neither knew how to get in. Eventually Isabel sat on the bank laughing while Daniel held the boat with the concentration of a man preventing an international incident.

On the lake, the rain became less noticeable. They paddled badly into an inlet where trees overhung the shore. Isabel took off her hood.

He remembered finding her wet hair inexplicably beautiful.

“We stole the key,” he said.

“Apparently.”

“We should return it.”

“I imagine they’ve managed.”

That evening they had eaten eggs and toast. Isabel talked about Peter. Daniel talked about Rachel, presenting himself as a man who had emerged from a sad but instructive experience.

He had not mentioned his relief when Rachel went away for work, or how that relief had frightened him.

Later, Isabel asked whether he would marry again.

“Possibly,” he said.

The grandeur of it embarrassed him now.

But he remembered something else. The cottage had a second bedroom, where they left their bags. Looking in one morning, he had felt astonishing contentment at the smooth bedspread and their luggage leaning together. They had arrived somewhere. There was another day before they had to leave.

“Why are you looking like that?” Isabel asked.

“Like what?”

“As though you’ve found a receipt for something expensive.”

“I’d forgotten the canoe.”

“I hadn’t.”

She picked up a broken umbrella and asked whether there was any reason to keep it.

Two weeks later, Daniel booked a canoe on the River Lea.

He did this before asking Isabel, producing a scheduling difficulty that a telephone call resolved.

“I can change it,” he said.

“I know. I’ve changed the other thing.”

The morning was bright and cold. An instructor explained how to paddle and told them not to stand up.

As they lowered themselves into the canoe, Daniel felt the familiar urge to suggest they watch someone else first. Then they were afloat.

They struck the bank twice.

“You’re steering,” Isabel said.

“I’m trying.”

“Those are different activities.”

Beyond the hire centre, warehouses stood behind reeds. A cyclist disappeared behind a hedge and emerged ahead, making their progress seem negligible.

Daniel began talking about the dream. He had imagined the outing would communicate something, sparing him the risk of saying it badly.

“I think part of what I like is that we haven’t lost the flat.”

“Although you don’t use it?”

“Yes.”

“That sounds like you.”

“I know.”

He let them drift.

“With Rachel, I thought there would be a better time. To move. To talk. After she left, I thought I’d learned something.”

“You did.”

“Not as much as I claimed.”

Isabel rested her paddle across her knees.

“I don’t want to be another thing you’re keeping for later.”

“You aren’t.”

“Sometimes I am.”

He wanted to explain the newspaper, the film, all the occasions on which his reluctance had been innocent.

“Yes,” he said.

They passed beneath a footbridge. Their strokes sounded briefly louder under the concrete. Beyond it, sunlight struck Isabel’s paddle.

That night he dreamed of the flat again. Rachel stood beside the kitchen window. The refrigerator had stopped humming.

He woke before anything was settled.

Beside him, Isabel asked the time. He told her. Soon she would ask again; she distrusted the clock on his side.

His shoulders ached from paddling. He moved closer, and without opening her eyes she reached back to draw his cold hand beneath the duvet.
